title: Coins: from odds to a hierarchical prior
promptMarkdown:
1. A friend's coin comes up heads seven times in a row. Compare $H_{\text{fair}}$ ($P(\text{H})=0.5$) with $H_{\text{trick}}$ ($P(\text{H})=0.95$) under a prior $P(H_{\text{trick}})=1/1000$. Compute the likelihood ratio, the posterior odds and $P(H_{\text{trick}}\mid D)$ to three significant figures.
2. What is the smallest number $n$ of consecutive heads after which the trick coin becomes more probable than the fair coin under this prior? Show the inequality you solve and check it with the integers on either side.
3. Now treat the weight $\theta$ as unknown with prior $\theta\sim\mathrm{Beta}(2,2)$ and observe 3 heads and 7 tails. Give the posterior distribution, the posterior predictive probability of heads on the next flip, the posterior mode, and the posterior standard deviation; compare the predictive with the maximum-likelihood estimate and explain the direction of the difference.
4. Hierarchical prior: $P(\text{fair})=0.99$; $\theta\mid\text{fair}\sim\mathrm{Beta}(1000,1000)$; $\theta\mid\text{unfair}\sim\mathrm{Beta}(1,1)$. For $D$ = 25 heads in a row, compute $P(D\mid\text{unfair})$ exactly, explain why $P(D\mid\text{fair})\approx2^{-25}$, and obtain an approximate posterior odds for fairness. The lecture reports about $9\times10^{-5}$; state whether your approximation is above or below the exact value and why.
hintLadder: Each head multiplies the odds by $P(\text{H}\mid\text{trick})/P(\text{H}\mid\text{fair})=1.9$. Posterior odds = likelihood ratio × prior odds, and prior odds are $1:999$.
For part 2 solve $1.9^n>999$ with logarithms, then check $n$ and $n-1$ directly.

The Beta posterior has parameters (prior heads + observed heads, prior tails + observed tails). Its mean is $\alpha/(\alpha+\beta)$, its mode $(\alpha-1)/(\alpha+\beta-2)$, its variance $\alpha\beta/\big((\alpha+\beta)^2(\alpha+\beta+1)\big)$.

$P(D\mid\text{unfair})=\int_0^1\theta^{25}\,d\theta$. For the fair branch, $\mathrm{Beta}(1000,1000)$ is concentrated very near $\tfrac12$; the exact value is $\prod_{i=0}^{24}\frac{1000+i}{2000+i}$, and each factor is slightly above $\tfrac12$.
